title: Find out which shell you use and which startup file to edit
summary: Check which shell runs in your terminal and which settings file it reads when it starts. Do this before you add an alias, a PATH entry or a variable, so you edit the right file. All checks only read information.

steps.explain: Show the login shell saved for your account. A new terminal usually starts this shell, but the window you are in may run another one. Read-only.
steps.expect: A path such as /bin/zsh (usual on macOS) or /bin/bash (usual on Linux).

steps.explain: Ask ps for the name of the program running this terminal, the process with ID $$. This is the shell you type into right now. Read-only.
steps.expect: bash or zsh. On macOS a login shell may show with a dash, such as -zsh. If you see 'ps: command not found', use the alternative.

alternatives.explain: Print the name the shell was started with. Works without ps. In an interactive terminal it matches the running shell.
alternatives.expect: bash or -zsh, the name of the shell in this window.

steps.explain: Check that the shell you plan to configure is installed. A settings file for a shell you do not have does nothing. Read-only.
steps.expect: A path such as /bin/zsh if zsh is installed. If it is missing, nothing is printed and the exit status is 1.

alternatives.expect: A path such as /bin/bash. If it is missing, nothing is printed.

steps.explain: List the startup files that already exist in your home folder. Pick the one for your shell: zsh uses ~/.zshrc; bash uses ~/.bashrc on Linux and ~/.bash_profile on macOS; ~/.profile is read by many shells for login settings. Edit only that file.
steps.cmd: for f in ~/.bashrc ~/.bash_profile ~/.profile ~/.zshrc ~/.zprofile; do [ -e "$f" ] && echo "$f"; done
steps.expect: Full paths such as /home/you/.bashrc, one per line, only for files that exist. Nothing printed means none exists yet; create the file when you first add a setting.
